blocks.text: Context that helps a model can also hurt you, because the same words that make a tool call smarter can carry a password, a customer record, or an internal file straight into the wrong hands.
MCP makes it easy to connect many servers to one conversation, and every one of those servers can, in principle, see everything the model has been shown so far.
This lesson is about the gap between what a server could see and what it actually needs to see, and how to close that gap on purpose instead of by accident.
1. What We Mean by a Context Leak

blocks.alt: A trusted server returns sensitive content which then sits in shared context unprotected

blocks.text: A context leak happens when information that entered a conversation for one purpose ends up visible to a party that had no business seeing it.
That party might be a different MCP server, a different tool on the same server, or even a different user sharing the same underlying session.
The leak is rarely dramatic. Usually it looks like ordinary context flowing exactly the way the system was built to let it flow, just further than anyone intended.
2. Context Has No Memory of Where It Came From
Once a resource has been read into the conversation, the text itself does not carry a label saying which server produced it or how sensitive it is.
The model sees a flat stream of tokens. A support ticket full of customer emails looks, to the model, exactly like any other paragraph of text sitting in context.

code.content:
# conceptually, everything collapses into one flat blob
assembled_context = system_prompt + resource_a_content + resource_b_content + tool_history
# nothing here marks resource_a_content as "internal only, do not forward"

blocks.text: 3. The Trust Boundary Problem

blocks.alt: Content crossing a trust boundary needs its own check

blocks.text: Every server you connect to an MCP host sits behind its own trust boundary. One server might be a first party internal tool, another might be a community plugin you barely know.
The moment a resource read from the trusted server sits in the same shared context as tool calls to the untrusted one, the boundary between them has effectively disappeared.

blocks.title: Trust is a property of the server, not of the content
blocks.content: A document does not become safer to share just because it already made it into context once. Every additional server it reaches is a new place that trust decision has to be made again.

blocks.text: 4. A Concrete Leak Scenario

blocks.alt: One server reads private data that another server then exposes to the model

blocks.text: Imagine an assistant connected to a company wiki server and a public web search server in the same session.
Early on, the user asks it to summarize an internal incident report, and the wiki server returns the full text, including customer names and account identifiers.

Later in the same conversation, the user asks the assistant to search the web for a related public issue. If the host blindly forwards full context to the search tool, those customer names can end up embedded in an outbound query string.
5. Why Blind Sharing Feels Convenient but Is Not Safe
Forwarding everything to every server is the easiest thing to build, which is exactly why it is the default a lot of early integrations reach for.
It also means the least trusted server you connect ends up with the same visibility as the most trusted one, which is the opposite of how trust is supposed to work.

items: A new, unaudited server gets the same view as a server you have used safely for years
A user has no way to know which of ten connected servers actually saw their sensitive question
Removing a server later does not undo whatever it already saw while connected

blocks.text: 6. Scoping Context to the Right Server

blocks.alt: Context is scoped so only the right server sees it

blocks.text: Scoping means deciding, for each piece of context, exactly which servers and tools are allowed to see it, instead of assuming the answer is always all of them.
A well scoped host keeps a per server view of the conversation, built from a shared history but filtered down before each individual call.

code.content:
def build_scoped_context(full_context, target_server):
    allowed_sources = server_permissions[target_server]["allowed_resource_sources"]
    return [
        item for item in full_context
        if item.source_server in allowed_sources
    ]

scoped = build_scoped_context(full_context, target_server="public_web_search")

blocks.text: 7. What a Scoping Policy Actually Looks Like
A scoping policy is just a table that maps each server to what it is allowed to receive, kept somewhere the host checks before every outbound call.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Server","Allowed to receive"],"rows":[["Internal wiki server","Only resources it produced itself, plus generic user questions"],["Public web search server","The current user question only, no internal resource content"],["Payment processor server","Only fields explicitly marked as payment relevant"]]}

blocks.text: Writing this table down forces a decision that blind forwarding lets you skip entirely.
8. Sanitizing Context Before It Travels

blocks.alt: Raw context is sanitized before it travels onward

blocks.text: Scoping decides who gets to see a piece of context at all. Sanitization decides what that piece of context is allowed to still contain once it is on its way.
Even a resource from a fully trusted server can carry details, like an internal database id or an email address, that a downstream tool never needed in the first place.
9. A Redaction Example
A simple sanitizer looks for known sensitive patterns, replaces them with a placeholder, and only then hands the result to the next server.
10. Sanitizing Structured Data, Not Just Prose
Tool results are often JSON, not free text, and a naive text based redaction pass can miss sensitive fields sitting inside structured objects.
Walking the actual object structure, field by field, catches things a regular expression over stringified text tends to miss.
11. What Sanitization Cannot Fix
Redaction is good at catching known patterns, an email shape, a key prefix, a labeled field. It is much weaker against sensitive information that has no fixed shape.
A paragraph describing a confidential business strategy in plain prose will sail straight through a pattern based sanitizer untouched.

blocks.title: Sanitization reduces risk, it does not eliminate it
blocks.content: Treat redaction as one layer among several, not as a single control you can rely on to catch everything sensitive.

blocks.text: 12. Multiple Users, One Context Store

blocks.alt: Multiple users sharing one context store need strict isolation between them

blocks.text: Many production MCP hosts back their sessions with a shared store, a database or cache holding conversation state for every active user at once.
That shared infrastructure is efficient to run, but it also means a bug in how sessions are keyed can put one user face to face with another user data.

code.content:
# the risky version: a lookup key that is easy to guess or collide on
session = context_store.get(session_id)
# if session_id is short, sequential, or not scoped to the authenticated user,
# a caller could request a different user's session by accident or on purpose

blocks.text: 13. Access Control at the Store Boundary
The fix is to treat the context store the same way you would treat any other multi tenant data store, with checks enforced at the boundary, not trusted to the caller.
Every read of shared context state should answer one question first: does this caller actually own this session.
14. Session Isolation in Practice
Isolation means a bug or a malicious request in one user session cannot read or modify another user session, even though both live in the same underlying store.

items: Give every session a long, random, unguessable identifier rather than a sequential one
Scope every query to the store by both session id and authenticated user id, never session id alone
Keep per user encryption keys or namespaces where the storage layer supports it
Expire and clear old sessions instead of letting stale context linger indefinitely

blocks.text: 15. Least Privilege as the Default Posture

blocks.alt: Minimum needed context is compared against granting everything by default

blocks.text: Least privilege means every server and every tool starts with access to nothing, and gains access only to what a specific task genuinely requires.
This is the opposite instinct from blind sharing, where the default is everything and restrictions get added later, usually after something has already gone wrong.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Posture","Starting point","Risk when misconfigured"],"rows":[["Blind sharing","Every server sees all context","One weak server exposes everything"],["Least privilege","No server sees anything by default","A missing grant blocks a feature, not a breach"]]}

blocks.text: 16. Logging and Auditing Context Flows
A scoping and sanitization policy is only as good as your ability to tell whether it actually held, which means every cross server context handoff deserves a log entry.
When something does leak, a clear audit trail is the difference between a quick fix and a long, uncertain investigation.
17. Trade-offs Between Convenience and Isolation

Strict scoping and sanitization cost something. A tool that would have benefited from a bit of extra background now has to work with less, and every new integration needs an explicit policy decision instead of just working out of the box.

That friction is the price of keeping a leak from turning into an incident. A slightly less capable tool call is almost always cheaper than a customer record ending up somewhere it never should have gone.
Worked Example
A support assistant connects to three servers, an internal ticket server, a billing server, and a public knowledge base search server.
A user asks it to look up their ticket, which pulls in their name, email, and a payment reference from the ticket server.

The user then asks the assistant to search the public knowledge base for a workaround. Under a scoping policy, the search call receives only the plain text question, not the ticket contents. Under a sanitization pass, even if ticket text were included, the email and payment reference would already be redacted before leaving the host.

code.content:
scoped_query = build_scoped_context(full_context, target_server="public_kb_search")
safe_query = sanitize(scoped_query)
result = mcp_client.call("public_kb_search.search", context=safe_query)

blocks.text: The result: the public search server never learns the customer name, email, or payment reference, even though that information was very much present earlier in the same conversation.
Common Mistakes

items: Forwarding the entire conversation context to every connected server by default, with no per server filtering.
Sanitizing free text but ignoring structured JSON fields that carry the same sensitive data.
Keying shared session state with short or sequential identifiers that are easy to guess or enumerate.
Checking session ownership only in the frontend and trusting the backend store to be safe by construction.
Treating a single redaction pass as complete protection instead of one layer in a larger design.
Never logging cross server context handoffs, which makes a leak nearly impossible to trace after the fact.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway
Context that enters a conversation for one reason can reach a server or a user that never should have seen it, unless something deliberately stops that from happening.
Scoping decides who gets to see a piece of context, sanitization decides what they see once they do, and access control keeps one session or user from ever reaching into another shared context store.
